OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Cursor are all sending webhooks now, and all four built them on Standard Webhooks, the open spec written by Svix. Downloads of the spec's npm package went from 1.7 million a month in September 2025 to 220 million a month at the moment.

This may be boring to hear for the nth time, but the reason is agents. An individual person checks on a running job a few times. An agent told to watch for changes checks every resource, every minute, for as long as it runs, and almost every one of those requests comes back with nothing latest. An agent that starts a job, polls until it finishes, and then starts the next one spends most of its time waiting: six steps with 15 seconds of polling each add 90 seconds, even when every operation is fast. Polling more often adds load, and polling less often adds delay, so there's not really a sweet spot.

Recent findings suggest that an event-driven API gets rid of that trade-off. It tells consumers when something changed or finished, so they stop asking. That matters most for work that runs for minutes or hours, like batch inference, fine-tuning, and video generation, and many APIs still don't offer it. Of the 57 AI APIs with long-running jobs that Svix reviewed for its State of Webhooks 2027 report, 19 make you poll for the result.

Webhooks are how most APIs push those events, and you can get a v1 out pretty fast. Making it dependable is an infrastructure problem, which is a class of problem that requires more time by default. Before you ship webhooks, you need an append-only event log behind every delivery, a fixed event format, signed payloads, retries with backoff, event IDs receivers can deduplicate on, per-endpoint isolation, and delivery logs your customers can read. If you skip one of these things, a customer is just going to bring it up later.

Each section below covers one of them with adaptable code, and Standard Webhooks works with existing verification libraries in most languages.

Sources indicate that if the request handler that changes the data also sends the webhook, a crash between the commit and the HTTP call loses the event, and nothing records that it should have gone out. A customer whose endpoint was down for longer than your retry window has no way to find out what they missed.

Both problems go away if you write each event to an append-only table, scoped per customer, in the same transaction as the change. Webhooks are delivered from that table, and the same table backs an HTTP endpoint customers can read from a cursor. Svix calls this design POKE (Publish Once, Kickoff Everywhere). Build the log first: a consumer who misses a webhook needs somewhere to resume from.

Every code path that changes state calls one helper inside its own transaction:.

Pass the helper the transaction handle. An insert through the connection pool commits separately, so you can end up with the event and no change, or the change and no event.

Recent findings suggest that the advisory lock prevents a subtler bug. Postgres assigns sequence values at insert time, but rows only become visible at commit. With two concurrent writers, a reader can see ID 102, store it as its cursor, and then never see ID 101 when the slower transaction commits. Holding a per-customer lock until commit makes each customer's events visible in ID order.

Reading the log is one indexed range query. The endpoint returns a cursor even when there are no new events, so a client can always store it and ask again later:.

authenticate stands in for the middleware that already protects your API and sets req.customerId. That scoping stops one customer from reading another's events. A customer who was offline for a week asks for events after their last cursor and gets everything they missed, in order. Publish your retention period, since it limits how far back that works. The same log can also serve synthetic created events for existing records when a upcoming integration needs to load its initial state.

Customers write handlers against your payloads, so you'll be supporting every field you ship.

Give each event an id, type, timestamp, and data. Use the log row's ID as the event ID so webhooks and the pull endpoint agree. Name types as a resource plus a past-tense action, like invoice.paid, and publish a catalog with an example payload for each type.

According to recent reports, emit an event for each state change a consumer would otherwise poll for. Deletions are the ones teams forget most. Long-running jobs need completion and failure events, such as export.completed and export.failed.

Recent findings suggest that adding a field is safe. Removing or renaming one breaks handlers, so ship a newly introduced type such as invoice.paid.v2 and keep sending the old one until customers have moved over.

Recent findings suggest that anyone who finds a customer's webhook URL can POST a fake invoice.paid to it. A signature lets the receiver confirm the request came from you, wasn't modified in transit, and isn't an old request being replayed.

Standard Webhooks signs the string id.timestamp.body with HMAC-SHA256, using a separate secret for each endpoint. Including the timestamp is what lets receivers reject old requests. Generate secrets with "whsec_" + crypto.randomBytes(24).toString("base64").

Send the result in three headers. The ID comes from the log and stays the same on every retry. The timestamp is the time of the current attempt, so each retry gets a newly introduced signature.

Receivers need the matching check, so put it in your docs:.

Recent findings suggest that the function takes the raw body because frameworks that parse JSON and serialize it again change the bytes, and the signature stops matching. It compares with crypto.timingSafeEqual, since === returns faster on an early mismatch and leaks timing information. It rejects requests more than five minutes old to block replays. The signature header is a space-separated list so that during a secret rotation you can send one signature per secret and the receiver accepts either.

That code highlights how the scheme works. In production, use a Standard Webhooks library on both ends. It implements the same algorithm:.

Receiving endpoints go down during deploys and outages, and they return errors when they're rate limited. If you only try once, each of those is a lost webhook.

Sources indicate that count any non-2xx response as a failure, redirects included. Following a redirect to an arbitrary host is a security problem in its own right. Count slow responses as failures too. The code below gives up after 15 seconds. Publish whatever limit you pick, because customer handlers have to respond within it.

These delays match the schedule Svix runs in production: eight attempts over a little more than 27 hours. The early retries cover restarts. The later ones give someone time to notice an outage and fix it. After each failure, pass the number of attempts so far to nextAttemptAt, and when it returns null, mark the delivery as failed. The event is still in the log, so once the customer fixes their server they can replay it or read it from the pull endpoint.

Store attempt state in a table next to the log. Timers in process memory disappear when the process restarts, and you don't need a message broker to avoid that.

In a recent development, decide what happens to endpoints that never come back. Svix disables an endpoint after five days of continuous failure and emits an event so the sender can tell the customer. Pick your own threshold, notify the customer when you disable their endpoint, and let them turn it back on.

Retries mean some events arrive twice. Usually the receiver processed the event but timed out before you saw its response, so you sent it again. Senders accept this at-least-once behavior because the alternative is dropping events, and receivers handle the duplicates.

Receivers deduplicate on webhook-id, which doesn't change between retries. The insert that stores the event can also be the duplicate check:.

webhook_inbox needs a text primary key id and a jsonb column payload. The handler verifies the signature, stores the event, and returns 204. A background worker processes the inbox, so the handler responds well within the sender's timeout. express.raw gives the route the unparsed body that verification needs.

Recent findings suggest that put this pattern in your docs with a note about ordering. Events in the log have a fixed order, but webhook deliveries don't always arrive in it. A retried invoice.created can land after invoice.paid. Receivers should keep whichever event has the newer updated_at, or read the pull endpoint when they need strict ordering.

With a shared worker pool, one customer's hanging endpoint can tie up every worker for the full timeout while other customers' events wait. Limit concurrent deliveries per endpoint, and slow down delivery to endpoints that keep failing.

According to recent reports, customer-supplied URLs are also an attack surface. Someone can register http://169.254.169.254/ or an internal hostname and get your servers to call your cloud metadata service or private network. This is server-side request forgery (SSRF). Resolve the hostname before connecting, reject private and loopback addresses, and don't follow redirects. The delivery code sets redirect: "manual" for this reason.

Without a self-serve view, every "did you send it?" question goes to an engineer who has to search logs.

It has been revealed that give customers a page to add and remove endpoints, choose event types, and rotate secrets. For each message, show every attempt with its timestamp, status code, and response body. The response body usually contains the customer's own error message. Add buttons to replay a failed message and to send a test event.

Expose the same operations in your API. Creating an endpoint and choosing its event types should take one authenticated request, because scripts and AI agents now set up a lot of integrations and can't click through a dashboard.

This is the biggest item here because it needs a UI, and it's the one teams most often leave out of the first release.

You can build all of this yourself, and many teams have. It comes down to the fact that it's cheap to manage delivery for 99% of your webhooks, but it's nontrivial to guarantee it for 100% of them. This is also ignoring the UX side such as offering the customer portal for your customers to manage their webhooks in.

Svix, which sponsored this article, handles webhook delivery. You keep the event log and decide what goes in it. A small relay reads latest rows and passes each one to Svix:.

Svix also hosts the debugging portal. This call returns a single-use link where the customer can manage endpoints, read delivery logs, and replay messages:.

The free tier includes 50,000 messages a month and doesn't require a credit card.

Before the first customer registers an endpoint, you should be able to answer yes to each of these:.

This year was a lot of things, but it was primarily a reminder that the best products are created through careful iteration. Only one product on this list, the XREAL Aura, represents an emerging class. The rest, from the Fitbit Air to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, showcase years of work in optimizing for design, weight, battery life, and performance. Some take more risks than others, but to us they all represent the very best of their respective categories.

A screenless Google device outside of a smart speaker wasn’t something I thought I needed. Yet the Fitbit Air has become one of my favorite products to come out of Mountain View in years. Fitness tracking is something I want happening quietly in the background, not another reason to check a screen.

That’s what the Air gets right. It isn’t trying to reinvent fitness tracking; it packages it in a comfortable, lightweight band that stays out of the way. Health tracking data isn’t locked behind a paywall, and there’s no display demanding attention throughout the day.

In a recent development, smart rings and full-featured watches have their place, but this slim wearable strikes a particularly appealing balance. It gives me useful information when I want it without becoming another device to manage. It’s comfortable, inexpensive, and easy to live with—and sometimes that’s exactly what makes a product great.

— Damien Wilde, Daniel Bader & Andrew Romero.

VRR support has made it possible to play my Steam Machine on a roughly 200-inch image in the bedroom, while the built-in speakers do an impressive job of filling the room. Going from Forza Horizon 5 at 120fps to Blue Planet on BBC iPlayer is effortless thanks to Google TV.

Sources indicate that the swiveling base is more useful than it might sound. I can position the projector in the corner of the room and let XGIMI’s keystone correction handle the rest. It’s an expensive upgrade, but for a home cinema setup that doubles as a giant gaming display, it’s a beast.

Price: $99Release date: May 4, 2026.

I still wish the Steam Controller cost less. Beyond that, though, I have very little to complain about: this is the best controller I’ve used in years. It’s comfortable, gives Windows owners a way to control their PC, and brings together some of the best ideas from my beloved Steam Deck.

Industry observers note that steam Input is the real selling point. The depth of customization makes this controller feel at home on a PC in a way few alternatives do. I haven’t connected with a newly introduced controller this quickly in a long time.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t mean everyone needs one. Most people would be well served by an 8BitDo controller—or even a Stadia controller converted to Bluetooth. But if you play on PC and want the premium option, this is my pick.

Its proportions feel more flexible than the square-shaped displays that have become so common across the category. — Ben Schoon, Daniel Bader & Andrew Romero.

ColorOS has quietly become one of the best Android experiences by getting the small details right, and the Ultra’s camera hardware and shooting experience remain standouts—even next to Oppo’s newer Find X10 Pro Max.

Sources indicate that this is one of those increasingly rare smartphones that feels unwilling to compromise. I’ll be thinking about it until there’s a proper successor, and the prospect of not getting one in 2027 is disappointing.

I wish Oppo had sold this phone officially in the US. Importing comes with real complications, but the Find X9 Ultra is one of the few phones good enough to make me consider it.

Price: ~$1,720Release date: March 13, 2026.

It’s been a remarkable year for foldables, but the Honor Magic V6 is my favorite of the bunch. Its combination of durability, battery life, and camera quality finally made me stop thinking about going back to a conventional slab phone.

The cameras are a big part of that. I used to rely entirely on my Panasonic GH5 for work photos; now I often reach for the Magic V6 instead. Its large 1/2-inch telephoto sensor helps it deliver the kind of dependable results I want when I need to capture something quickly.

According to recent reports, it’s also held up to far more punishment than I’d normally put a foldable through. After a mud torture test and a trip through the dishwasher, I’m still using it months later. Battery life has been another major strength.

Honor’s software still has rough edges, but the improvements are substantial, and the seven-year update promise matters. The remaining problem is availability: I’d love to see Honor make its phones officially accessible across North America.

Price: $1,099Release date: November 2026.

Android XR has had an awkward start, but the XREAL Aura feels like the kind of product the platform needed from the beginning. It puts a fresh idea into a form factor that’s easier to imagine wearing than a bulky headset.

Think of it as smart glasses that behave more like a VR headset. Open the app drawer with a pinch—or use the tethered compute puck—and your chosen app appears as a floating window you can move around. It’s like having a tablet suspended wherever you need it.

It has been revealed that that makes remote work and entertainment feel surprisingly natural, especially when the glasses weigh less than a fifth of many VR headsets. There are compromises: hand gestures can be finicky, and while Bluetooth game controllers work, there isn’t a Meta Quest-style motion controller available for immersive gaming.

It has been revealed that even so, Aura makes a compelling case for Android XR. It’s an appealing option for people interested in immersive entertainment who don’t want the weight and bulk of a conventional VR headset.

Sources indicate that droidDeck has changed the way I think about gaming on Android. It isn’t the first project to bring PC games to a phone, but it feels like one of the most capable. The pitch is straightforward, even if the technology isn’t: run Steam on your Android device.

According to recent reports, rather than emulating an entire PC in the traditional sense, DroidDeck brings together translation layers using projects such as FEX and Proton. The technical details are complicated, but the practical result is that your phone can run games it wasn’t originally designed to understand.

Performance across my devices has been impressive—good enough that I’ve seen games run better than on my Steam Deck. The project is also free, community-driven, and highly customizable. The trade-off is that support for brand-new hardware can take time.

If you’ve been on the fence about mobile gaming, pairing DroidDeck with a controller such as my favorite, the GameSir G8 Galileo, is a great way to see how far it’s come.

#230308. Breaking: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (646 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Googleblog ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I help lead Google's agent skills program, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills.
  • Sources indicate that in Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out.
  • In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I help lead Google's agent skills program, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter.

Sources indicate that in Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and Gemini 4 Argon translated the path to each trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint.

In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.

Recent findings suggest that A recent post from Anthropic highlighted how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked Rocq proofs across OSS-Fuzz libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function.

It has been revealed that in C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to runtime.panicBounds that panics, crashing the process unless recovered.

Before generating machine code, Go's SSA prove pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the runtime.panicBounds traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target.

It has been revealed that I compiled each target with GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64 go build -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1" (-S prints the assembly listing and ssa/check_bce/debug=1 logs every surviving bounds check) and passed both the Go source and the disassembly to the model. Looking at Go source alone, you can't see which bounds checks the compiler already removed or where a register gets truncated to 8 bits; in the disassembly, both show up. I targeted RISC-V because it's the instruction set Anthropic's post targets for its Rocq proofs, and Go cross-compiles to it out of the box.

Industry observers note that from there, Argon read the Go source and disassembly and returned a Z3 script modeling the path to each surviving trap, along with a patched function whenever it flagged a bug. Z3 then checked whether those constraints could be satisfied, and whenever it found a crashing input, go test replayed those bytes against the real function. Using an LLM saved me from translating assembly into solver constraints by hand. Argon's translation dominated the runtime, at about a minute per function, while Z3 itself finished in milliseconds.

It’s hard to believe we finally got a proper premium phone from Motorola again, and it feels a bit like the return of the Moto X.

Motorola’s slow regeneration in North America from a mostly budget device-minded company to one offering the most expensive non-folding flagship phone might become the thing of legend. That’s not to say the company hasn’t shown true greatness in the past — the Moto X, Moto Z, and Razr lines are proof of that — but it’s always shied away from pulling out all the stops until the Motorola Signature 27 arrived.

It has been revealed that freshly unboxed and sitting in my hands, the textile-clad Capulet Olive Motorola Signature 27 colorway has impressed me in every way, shape, and form over the past 24 hours. It’s a much longer period of time than I usually get with hands-on opportunities and, yet, the newness of the experience has yet to wear off.

Industry observers note that part and parcel to that experience is the design. For whatever reason, this is the year Motorola seems to have truly figured out what makes a phone nice to hold. The textile back, ribbed metal frame, rounded corners, and curved edges on the front and back of the phone are purely blissful to hold. It’s a reminder that a phone can be as good looking as it feels instead of being a flat, boring, off-balance slab like too many phones are now.

The weight also surprised me. On paper this sits right in the middle of all the Ultra/Pro Max-named phones, yet it feels lighter for some intangible reason. The camera hump makes it slightly top-heavy, and it’s almost as wobble-free as a Pixel (there’s just one off-center camera hump).

It has been revealed that the new 120Hz LTPO tandem OLED display is as top-notch as you’re going to get. I had all of maybe 2 hours of direct sunlight yesterday to test it with, and boy does it ever get bright. The rest of the time, I’ve been either inside or out in overcast weather, all of which it looked brilliant in. And it uses a combination of DC dimming above 20% brightness, and 2160Hz PWM dimming below 20% brightness, making it super comfortable for me.

Motorola’s software has evolved again with this release, and the verdict is still out on whether or not this is actually better than the firm’s Android 16 designs. The build of Android 17 that ships with this phone utilizes some major design changes we’ve only seen on a few random low-end Motorola phones, and I’m not sure I care for the gentle gradients on the quick toggle icons and some other system UI elements. It feels like a weirdly cheap effect that clashes with Material Design’s flatter motif.

It has been revealed that despite that, this is the most Pixelly (is that a word?) a Motorola phone has ever felt. Features like Rambler, Sign to Text, and Create My Widget are here and work impeccably well. Gemini Intelligence is also on the way, and while there’s no specific ETA for that at the moment, it’s exciting to know that the most advanced Android features — which are currently only available on a very small number of devices — are coming to this phone.

This may also be the fastest phone I’ve used to date. Everything is unbelievably snappy. Tap an icon and the thing opens instantly. Animations are zippy, and the fresh lock screen and customization options feel cohesive. Plus, all the favorite Moto actions and gestures are still here, which I greatly appreciate.

Sources indicate that I’ve got some lofty expectations for this camera hardware, too, and it’s because Motorola is talking up such a big game. DXOMark’s camera review rated it the 2nd-best smartphone camera in the world, just under the Huawei Pura 80 Ultra and above the iPhone 18 Pro. Some people don’t take much stock in DXOMark, but it’s still worth noting that they’ve praised the heck out of the camera and Motorola is also pushing this as a winner in a way they’ve never done before.

Recent findings suggest that the hype for the Motorola Signature 27 certainly seems to be realized, and now only time will truly tell if it can live up to the lofty expectations Motorola’s $1,599 price has set for it. If nothing, it’s certainly off to a good start and has made an excellent first impression.

Beijing’s AI ambitions are under threat as models may fall behind by up to nine months versus competitors — Chinese AI labs are under heavy fire from export controls, maturing chip stacks and a distillation crackdown

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models.
  • Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters noted.
  • Recent findings suggest that these curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models. In September, Mozilla estimated that open-weight AI models were three to six months behind the frontier. Since then, developments in the AI industry and export control rules could mean that Chinese AI models, many of which are typically open-weight, might fall even further behind Western counterparts, by up to nine months.

Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters noted. It's an open secret that data centers located in Asia have been renting compute capacity to Chinese entities for some time. In light of the recent Nvidia scandal involving Jensen Huang and Megaspeed, the U.S. Department of Commerce has since tightened its rules over how data centers lend their compute capacity to Chinese entities. This has created an environment where there is, in fact, an excess of compute capacity available in the region, Bloomberg reported.

Recent findings suggest that these curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region. However, this isn't entirely true across the industry. DeepSeek is attempting to wean itself off foreign silicon and instead adopting Huawei's Ascend AI chips, and porting its libraries away from CUDA and onto the open-source CANN. However, this hasn't stopped Chinese AI labs from facing another concern: tightened security against the distillation of AI models.

Distillation is a practice wherein the way a model thinks can be extracted and then learned from. It is largely believed to be the method in which Chinese AI labs have made great leaps in intelligence over the past several years, though several of China's leading labs refute that claim. The Western frontier has become more obtuse: Anthropic in October detailed how it's leveled up its own defences against distillation attacks, and the obfuscation of an AI model's chain of thought adds another hurdle. According to The Information, this is an problem that DeepSeek is now reportedly reckoning with. If distillation curbs the development of Chinese AI models even further, the gap between Eastern and Western frontier intelligence grows from three to six months to an estimated nine months.

If you look at Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, which ranks AI models across a wide range of benchmarks and scores them in numerical order, Anthropic currently has the leading public AI model: Claude Fable 5.2, at a total of 65 points. Meanwhile, the leading Chinese AI model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, sits at 47. Between the two contenders are practically every Western frontier lab: OpenAI, Google, and Meta are all outgunning Chinese competitors, which were, just a few short months ago, competing at the frontier across many tasks.

Recent findings suggest that it's vital to mention that Artificial Analysis also changed its methodology over recent weeks, with China's AI models falling slightly further behind in added benchmarks, such as the Omniscience score, which tracks how often an AI is likely to hallucinate. This is paired with a jump in capability among the Western labs: Right now, it's on the Chinese AI labs' shoulders to respond in kind, and if current releases are anything to go by, they are falling short of expectations, especially in domains such as cybersecurity. An Epoch AI report characterized the difference in capabilities between GLM 5.3 and Claude Opus 5.5 as a six-to-seven-month gap in intelligence. With the release of newer models like Claude Fable 5.2, it's likely that gap has only widened, and the same story is likely to play out over the next few months across additional domains.

With additional safeguards against distillation and powerful compute resources becoming more difficult to find, this poses a difficult question for the Chinese labs: How can they keep up the pace and stay competitive while the odds are stacked against them?

China still holds the overall top spot in the open-weight arena with Kimi K3.1 Pro, though Western companies are bringing more performant models out as the months pass. China's second tier of open-weight models, which can often be run locally, e.g Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-27B (20 on AA), is facing competition from the American-made Thinking Machines Labs' Inkling 2 Mini (20 on AA), which was recently released. With the release of the larger (closed-weight and API only) Qwen 4 model seemingly not landing quite as well with consumers, it remains to be seen whether Alibaba can maintain the advantage of time, as Inkling 2 Mini was released just this week, while Qwen 3.8-27B has been out for several months.

With devices like the RTX Spark, AMD's AI Halo, and more, owners are increasingly getting their own choice of running an open-weight AI, and for all intents and purposes, that usually means using a Chinese model to get the most intelligence out of your machine. However, recent developments show that smaller Western labs are also beginning to bridge that gap.

Sources indicate that this is yet another arena in which Chinese and Western labs will want to wrest control from one another. Notably, Google has not released another series of Gemma models following Gemma 4 back in April. If a fifth generation of Google's Gemma models arrives, they'd likely be close cousins to the Gemini Neon, Carbon, Argon, and Hydrogen family, though that remains speculation until Google confirms anything official.

Against the backdrop of export controls and tightening restrictions on AI distillation, Chinese AI labs are in a tough spot, and all eyes are on frontier labs like Moonshot AI, Zhipu, Deepseek, Alibaba, and Xiaomi to see if they can scale the intelligence wall that their Western counterparts currently present. More compute for training resources may be an answer, but for comparison's sake, Huawei's upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator offers 2 PFLOPS of FP4 compute and 1 PFLOPS of FP8, while an Nvidia Rubin R200 offers 50 PFLOPS in inference and 35 PFLOPS in dense workloads. In memory capacity and bandwidth, the Ascend 950DT can offer 144GB of HiZQ 2.0 with 4 TB/s of bandwidth across a 2 TB/s interconnect. Rubin, on the other hand, offers 288GB of HBM4, with bandwidth ranging from 19.2-22 TB/s, across an NvLink interconnect at 2.6 TB/s.

Recent findings suggest that if China's AI ambitions are to compete with the West, its silicon needs to either scale so the country can produce more chips to outgun a Western AI deployment with sheer numbers, or it needs to develop more advanced accelerators, while also managing the CANN software stack. The chips are figuratively, and literally, stacked heavily against China. As the race to develop Artificial Intelligence marches on, the Department of Commerce's latest measures have undoubtedly made it incredibly difficult for the country to compete.

Sources indicate that building a website involves more than writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Developers also need to test how their code behaves in different browsers, identify layout problems, investigate JavaScript errors, and understand why certain pages take longer to load.

Recent findings suggest that browser developer tools make these tasks easier. They provide a way to inspect the code right now running in a browser without constantly changing files or guessing what might be wrong.

Whether you're developing a new website or maintaining an existing application, learning to use these tools can improve your debugging workflow and help you write more reliable code.

Let's explore some useful browser development tools and how to apply them to everyday web development tasks.

Browser developer tools, commonly called DevTools, are built-in utilities available in modern browsers such as Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, and Safari.

They allow developers to examine a webpage's HTML structure, modify CSS properties, debug JavaScript, inspect network requests, and test responsive layouts.

Recent findings suggest that you can usually open them by right-clicking a webpage and selecting Inspect. On Windows and Linux, the F12 key or Ctrl + Shift + I shortcut also opens DevTools in most browsers.

The following table highlights some commonly used features:.

Understanding what each panel does makes it easier to select the right tool for a particular problem.

The Elements panel is one of the most frequently used features in browser DevTools.

Industry observers note that it displays the Document Object Model (DOM), which represents the structure of the webpage right now loaded in the browser. Developers can select individual elements and examine the CSS rules affecting their appearance.

It has been revealed that for example, imagine that a heading has more spacing than expected. Instead of immediately editing the stylesheet, inspect the heading and review its computed styles.

You might discover that the spacing comes from a margin inherited through another CSS rule or from a conflicting selector.

You can also experiment with CSS properties directly inside DevTools.

If the card appears too wide, you can temporarily change its width or padding in the Styles panel.

The browser immediately displays the result, allowing you to compare different values without repeatedly editing and saving your stylesheet.

Sources indicate that however, these temporary changes do not automatically revision your original CSS files. Once you've identified the correct solution, apply it to your project source code.

For more detailed CSS debugging techniques, developers can also read SitePoint's guide on CSS Debugging and Optimization: Browser-based Developer Tools.

JavaScript errors can prevent interactive features from working correctly. A navigation menu might stop opening, a form might fail to submit, or a button might not trigger the expected action.

The Console panel helps developers investigate these problems.

For example, consider the following JavaScript:.

If the page does not contain an element with the ID submitButton, the selected value will be null. Calling addEventListener() on that value causes an error.

You can prevent this particular problem by checking whether the element exists:.

The Console panel also allows developers to execute JavaScript expressions manually.

This returns the number of image elements currently present in the document.

You can use similar expressions to inspect elements, check values, and test small pieces of functionality.

Sometimes a JavaScript error is not immediately visible. A function may execute successfully but produce an unexpected result.

In such cases, the Sources panel in Chrome DevTools or the Debugger panel in Firefox can help.

Industry observers note that A breakpoint pauses JavaScript execution at a specific line. Developers can then inspect variable values, examine the call stack, and execute the code step by step.

If the application displays an incorrect total, you can place a breakpoint inside calculateTotal().

When the function executes, the browser pauses and allows you to inspect the values of price, quantity, and total.

This is more useful than repeatedly adding console.log() statements throughout a large application.

Breakpoints are particularly helpful when debugging complex functions, asynchronous operations, and event handlers.

A webpage may contain several resources, including images, stylesheets, JavaScript files, fonts, and API requests.

If one of these resources fails to load, part of the website may stop working correctly.

The Network panel provides information about requests made by the browser.

It displays request URLs, HTTP status codes, response sizes, loading times, and other useful details.

For example, the following table explains some common HTTP responses developers may encounter:.

Suppose an image is missing from a product page. Open the Network panel, reload the page, and filter the requests by images.

If the image returns a 404 response, check whether the file path is correct and whether the resource exists on the server.

The same process can help investigate failed API requests.

For example, if a frontend application requests product information from an API, the Network panel allows you to inspect the request method, response status, and returned data.

This helps developers distinguish between frontend problems and backend errors.

A website that looks correct on a desktop computer may not work properly on a smartphone.

Text can overflow, navigation menus can become difficult to use, and images may extend beyond their containers.

Browser DevTools include responsive design and device emulation features that allow developers to test different viewport sizes.

In Chrome, you can enable the device toolbar from the DevTools interface. Firefox provides a similar feature called Responsive Design Mode.

The desktop layout displays three columns, while smaller screens display one column.

You can test this behavior by changing the viewport width inside DevTools.

A useful responsive testing process includes:.

Checking common mobile and tablet widths.

Testing both portrait and landscape orientations.

Looking for horizontal scrolling.

Checking whether navigation remains usable.

Verifying that buttons and links are easy to interact with.

Device emulation is useful during development, but it does not completely replace testing on physical devices.

A website can have correct HTML, CSS, and JavaScript but still provide a poor experience if it loads slowly or performs unnecessary work.

The Performance panel helps developers investigate browser activity over time.

It can record page interactions and provide information about scripting, rendering, painting, and other browser operations.

For example, a page might become unresponsive when a user opens a navigation menu. A performance recording can help identify whether a long-running JavaScript function is blocking the main thread.

Developers can also use tools such as Lighthouse to audit performance, accessibility, SEO, and other aspects of a webpage.

Instead of making random optimization changes, use the available measurements to identify the actual problem.

Some useful areas to investigate include:.

Unnecessary JavaScript execution.

Excessive layout recalculations.

Performance analysis should be repeated after making changes to determine whether the optimization actually improves the result.

These features are useful, but they can also introduce debugging challenges.

For example, an application might continue displaying outdated information because an old value remains stored in local storage.

The Application panel in Chrome DevTools allows developers to inspect and manage several types of browser storage.

Consider this simple JavaScript example:.

If the application behaves unexpectedly because of stored data, inspecting local storage can help identify the problem.

Be careful when clearing storage because doing so may remove authentication sessions, saved preferences, or other application data.

Knowing individual DevTools features is useful, but developers benefit even more from using them in a consistent order.

The following workflow can make troubleshooting more efficient:.

This process helps developers identify the cause of a problem before changing multiple parts of the application.

It also makes debugging easier when working with other developers because the issue can be reproduced and explained using specific observations.

Recent findings suggest that browser developer tools are essential for modern web development. They help developers inspect HTML and CSS, debug JavaScript, analyze network requests, test responsive layouts, and investigate performance issues.

The most effective approach is to select the appropriate tool for the problem instead of making changes based on assumptions.

Whether you're working on a small website or a complex web application, becoming familiar with DevTools can make your development workflow more efficient and help you build websites that are easier to maintain.

Recent findings suggest that rather than treating debugging as something that happens only after development, make it a regular part of your workflow. This allows you to identify problems earlier, verify your solutions, and deliver more reliable web experiences.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola has been content with mid-grade haptics for years, but the Motorola Signature 27’s haptics rightfully upgrade the experience.

Two days ago, I unboxed the Motorola Signature 27 and talked about my experience a bit in my Motorola Signature 27 hands-on. It’s as gorgeous as the pictures make it look, and the texture on the back of my “Capulet Olive” green colorway is the stuff of dreams. But the thing that sealed the upcoming ultra-high-quality design for me wasn’t the comfortable curved edges or the textile back: it was the haptic motors.

In a recent development, now, don’t get me wrong. The Motorola Signature 27’s build and design are probably my favorite of the year. I’ll need to use it for just a bit longer to be 100% sure, but the pebble-like aesthetic of the curved front, back, and edges feels tangibly amazing to hold and use. It reminds me a bit of the Galaxy S3’s design, just without the nasty, slimy plastic back. It’s curved just enough to feel amazing, but not enough to be an annoyance like some waterfall display phones were in the past.

But a haptic motor is completely intangible to you as the reader. You can’t see it in pictures, and even if I describe it, you may not fully understand why it makes such a difference. If you’ve been using Google Pixel phones for a long time, you’ve probably forgotten how good a quality haptic motor can feel, but let me remind you for a moment just how important such an invisible thing can be to completing the experience.

Sources indicate that typing on the Signature 27 is pure bliss because of it. Tapping each key feels more like the press of a physical keyboard key. Unlocking the phone emits a satisfying light punch to my thumb, signalling a successful read. When I send a reply on X (Twitter), the button tap and subsequent animation feel like the message is being sent through the phone onto the web. It’s wonderful, and it’s one of the reasons people love the Pixel experience so much.

Unfortunately, the Motorola Signature 27’s haptic responses aren’t applied to as many parts of the UI as Pixel phones do, and that’s where the real miss comes in. Adjusting the brightness or volume doesn’t feel like a physically rotating vertical dial the way it does on Pixel, and I’d love to see Motorola add this in an patch. But at least the upgraded haptic engine is a huge step in the right direction for Motorola and a good way to make the Signature 27 feel like a proper flagship phone.

According to recent reports, A mobile app sends POST /orders. The server creates the order, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app sees a timeout and retries. Now the customer has two orders, and your support team has a refund to process.

Sources indicate that retrying is the right thing for a client to do. The problem is that POST is not idempotent: RFC 9110 defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods, but not POST or PATCH. Repeating a POST can repeat its side effects.

Recent findings suggest that an idempotency key fixes this. The client generates a unique key for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server does the work once, stores the response against the key, and returns the stored response for any retry. The IETF HTTPAPI working group is standardizing this pattern as the Idempotency-Key HTTP header field, and this tutorial follows its recommendations.

It has been revealed that we'll build it with Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL. By the end you'll have a table that stores keys, a function that safely claims a key under concurrent requests, an Express route that replays stored responses, and a client that retries without creating duplicates.

It has been revealed that the client's job is simple: generate a key, usually a UUID, and send the same key on every retry of the same operation. The draft defines the header value as a quoted string:.

The server's job is harder, because every request falls into one of five cases:.

Sources indicate that to tell case 3 from case 4, the server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key. A matching fingerprint means a genuine retry; a different one means key reuse. Case 5 is the one most implementations get wrong, because it only shows up under concurrency. A database constraint handles it for us.

Create a project and install the two dependencies:.

The key table records who sent the key, the request fingerprint, whether the work has finished, and the response to replay:.

In a recent development, two details matter here. The primary key includes client_id, so keys are scoped per client: two customers who happen to generate the same value can't see each other's responses. And locked_until lets the server recover a key whose request crashed halfway, which we'll use in Step 3.

Sources indicate that the draft defines the header value as a structured field string, which means it arrives wrapped in double quotes. Many clients send it without quotes, so the parser below accepts both and limits the characters and length it will store:.

In a recent development, the fingerprint has to be identical for identical requests, even if a client serializes the JSON body with its properties in a different order. Sorting object keys before hashing takes care of that. The hash uses SHA-256 from Node's built-in crypto module:.

Including the method and path means a key reused on a different endpoint counts as a mismatch, not as a retry.

In a recent development, the tempting approach is to SELECT the key, and insert it if nothing comes back. Under concurrency that fails: two retries arriving a few milliseconds apart both see no row, and both do the work.

Sources indicate that instead, let the primary key decide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING either inserts the row or does nothing, atomically, even across many application processes. The PostgreSQL INSERT documentation describes this behavior in detail. If the insert returns a row, this request owns the key. If not, we read the existing row and decide which case we're in:.

Sources indicate that the UPDATE in the last step is also atomic. If two retries find the same expired lock, only one of them matches the locked_until < now() condition and gets the key. If the row disappears between the two queries, for example because it was released after a failure, the function reports in_progress and the client simply retries.

Set LOCK_SECONDS comfortably above the slowest time your operation takes. If the lock expires while the original request is still running, a retry can take over and run the work a second time.

Industry observers note that once a request owns the key, it creates the order and marks the key as completed. Both writes happen in one transaction, so there is no moment where the order exists but the key still notes in_progress, or the other way round. Note that a transaction in node-postgres has to use a single client checked out from the pool, as the node-postgres transaction documentation explains:.

Recent findings suggest that releaseKey runs when the work fails. Deleting the claim lets the client retry with the same key instead of waiting for the lock to expire. It only deletes rows that are still in progress, so a completed response is never thrown away.

In a recent development, the route validates the body first. A request with invalid input never touches the key table, so the client can fix the input and resend with the same key. Error responses use the application/problem+json format from RFC 9457, which the idempotency draft also uses in its examples:.

Recent findings suggest that the server side only works if the client keeps the key stable. The most common client bug is generating a new key inside the retry loop, which turns every retry into a new operation. Generate the key once per logical action, before the first attempt:.

The catch branch is the reason idempotency keys exist. After a timeout, the client can't know whether the order was created. With a stable key, retrying is safe either way: if the first attempt succeeded, the retry returns the stored order; if it didn't, the retry creates it. The random jitter spreads retries out, so many clients recovering from the same outage don't all hit the server at once.

Sources indicate that in a browser or mobile app, store the key with the pending action, for example in the form state or a local queue. If the user taps "Place order" again after an error, reuse it. Only generate a latest key when the user starts a genuinely new action.

According to recent reports, keys can't live forever, or the table grows without limit. The draft leaves the retention period to the server but says it should be published in the API documentation, so clients know how long a retry stays safe. Twenty-four hours covers most retry scenarios. A scheduled job can delete older rows in batches:.

Recent findings suggest that run it every few minutes from cron or your job scheduler until it deletes zero rows. Deleting in batches keeps each transaction short, and the created_at index from Step 1 keeps the inner query fast. A retry that arrives after its key has expired is treated as a fresh request, which is why the retention period belongs in your documentation.

Start the server with node server.js, then send the same request twice:.

It has been revealed that the second request lists the properties in a different order, and it's still recognized as a retry because of the canonical fingerprint. Both responses carry the same order ID, and the orders table contains one row.

Recent findings suggest that now change the quantity while keeping the key. The server answers 422, because the key now belongs to a different request:.

To see the concurrent case, add await newly introduced Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000)); before completeKey in the route, restart the server, and fire two requests with a new key at the same time:.

One request prints 201 and the other 409. Without the ON CONFLICT claim, both would have printed 201 and created two orders. Remove the delay when you're done.

According to recent reports, this design guarantees that the database work in Step 4 happens once per key. Two situations need extra care:.

It has been revealed that idempotency keys don't replace other safeguards either. A unique constraint on a natural business key, such as one payment per invoice, still catches duplicates that arrive with different keys, for example when a user submits the same form from two tabs.

With one table, an atomic claim and a transaction that stores the response next to the work, POST endpoints become safe to retry. Clients get a simple rule: generate one key per action, reuse it on every retry. The server takes care of the rest, including the concurrent retries that a SELECT-then-INSERT approach misses.

The same pattern works for PATCH endpoints and for webhooks you send to other systems. Start with the endpoints where a duplicate costs real money or confuses a customer, and publish your key format and retention period in the API documentation so client developers know what to send.

Garmin and Bark are competing for your money this year, and these sales make it easy to get something fun that’ll keep your kids safe and in touch.

It has been revealed that if you’re anything like me, you didn’t give your kids a phone or tablet the second they were out of the womb. Instead, I’ve slowly introduced them to personal devices as I felt it made sense, and a smartwatch was one of the first easy ways for them to stay in touch while away from home without being introduced to the dangers of the internet. This year’s Black Friday sales on Bark and Garmin kids’ smartwatches slash up to $64 off the regular price, making them an easier decision than ever to pick up.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve tested a lot of kids’ smartwatches over the years, and I can easily recommend the two in the picture above: the Bark Watch and the Garmin Bounce 2. Choosing between the two is easy enough. Garmin’s watch is simpler and comes in a slightly more durable case with fun colors. It’s slightly cheaper than Bark, but doesn’t have any health sensors on board. It mainly tracks steps, allows your kids to message or call you, and gives you geofencing and location tracking through a $9.99 per month LTE subscription plan. It’s got a 5ATM rating and a polycarbonate case, so it’s quite durable.

Sources indicate that the Garmin Bounce 2 is preloaded with a few mini games and educational apps, plus the Garmin Jr. app has built-in unlockables and rewards parents can set for doing chores, completing schoolwork, etc. Battery life is roughly 2 days with normal use, but can be less if you’re in an area with poor LTE reception. The Garmin Bounce 2 is best for kids 10 and under.

Industry observers note that the Bark Watch uses Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 hardware and a custom version of Wear OS. It’s a much more powerful watch and only gets a day of battery life because of it. This one feels like a midpoint between a kids’ watch and a standard Wear OS watch, as it has all the power of Wear OS but doesn’t feature the Google Play Store. It doesn’t have any games, social media, or browsers.

Since it uses Samsung’s hardware, it includes cutting-edge health sensors that your kids can use, plus great multitasking and a svelte, attractive design. Bark charges $15 per month for its plan, which includes a Bark App subscription for the whole family. I also use the Bark App on my son’s phone, which helps me monitor his usage and make sure he’s safe online. The extra $5 per month adds up, but it’s absolutely worth it if you want to add the Bark App to another phone or tablet.

The Bark Watch is fine enough for younger kids, but the design and lack of games feel more like an “older kids’ watch” to me, and my 12-year-old son agrees. Either way you go, these are fantastic choices that you’ll be happy with, especially with a nice little deal.

In a recent development, this gaming-friendly external power button has a 2-meter (78.74 inch) cable, along with a splitter that lets you connect both buttons to your case's front panel buttons. It also includes adhesive pads and zip-ties.

Industry observers note that simple enough, then, but that's not to downplay what you're getting here, or how it's been made. Mechanical keyboard keys are an interesting choice, because they look like they've been plucked straight from a top-spec gaming keyboard, especially with the RGB lighting underneath. It's a showstopper by design. SinLoon could have just gone for a massive, round button, but by going for a design that uses mechanical keyboard keys, they're making sure this button has longevity.

Sources indicate that that's why SinLoon reckons these keys are good for no less than five million keystrokes. You can switch your PC on or off five million times before this board wears out. That's a lot of restarts. The two keys themselves sit in a smooth, black plastic case. The wiring is black, too, and sheathed (mostly) in glossy plastic, extending from the back. It does eventually split into different colored cables, though, each labeled so you know their purpose and where you'll need to connect them.

While you will need to open up your PC to get this installed, it's an easy enough process, as long as your case lets you get close to your PC's front panel headers. PC builders won't have much trouble with this, as you've probably already dealt with these cables when you've hooked it up to your motherboard. It's the same process for these cables, and it comes with connectors to handle the power and disk access LEDs, too.

Recent findings suggest that you don't have to sacrifice your PC's power buttons, either. This SinLoon power button comes with a 1-to-2 splitter, a physical adapter that lets you connect these cables alongside the cables handling your PC's power and reset buttons. It's a physical adapter, so if the pinout doesn't quite match up, you can just move the header cables around until it works. For photographers, videographers and content creators, an SD card is more than a storage device. It holds the raw material behind a finished project: wedding photographs, travel footage, product demos and drone recordings that may be impossible to recreate. Data loss can happen at almost any stage of that workflow, from a folder deleted to make space to a card formatted before the footage was backed up.

This article explains why files on a card become unavailable, what to do in the first minutes, how recovery tools find data, and how to compare options. It includes a small Python example that recovers JPEG files from a disk image, so you can see the mechanism for yourself. It also compares free open-source tools with paid graphical ones, using criteria you can apply yourself. Recovery is never guaranteed, and tool features change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

Recovery is not just a matter of finding a deleted filename. Several different problems can make files unavailable, and they call for different approaches.

These steps cannot guarantee recovery, but they reduce avoidable risk.

Most tools combine two methods, and understanding them helps you read scan results.

According to recent reports, carving has a cost. Because file system information is ignored, names and folder structure are usually lost, which is why scan results often show generic names. Fragmented files can also be recovered incomplete, since the tool assumes the pieces are stored one after another. Free tools build on these same ideas. Wondershare Recoverit V15, which also offers a free version for Windows and Mac, adds a graphical interface, while PhotoRec and ddrescue stay closer to the command line.

The script below is a teaching sketch, not a recovery product. It reads a raw disk image, finds JPEG start markers, and writes out the bytes up to the last end marker before the next start. That detail matters because a JPEG can contain an embedded thumbnail with its own markers, so stopping at the first end marker would cut a file short.

A short test builds two real JPEGs, hides them in random bytes, and checks that both are carved and open as valid images:.

Use it on an image rather than the card itself. On Linux you can make one with a read-only copy, for example with the GNU ddrescue tool, which is designed to copy data from failing media. Then run the carver against the image and save the output to a different drive. Real tools handle many more formats, trim files using header information, and deal with video containers, so treat this as a way to understand the idea.

In a recent development, the right choice depends on the problem, your platform and how comfortable you are with the command line. The table summarizes what each project’s own documentation states.

The order of steps matters more than the choice of tool. A cautious workflow on Linux or macOS looks like this:.

Graphical tools follow the same logic and mainly change step 3, with thumbnails, filters and search that make large result sets easier to browse. Whether that is worth paying for depends on how many files you need to sift through and how comfortable you are on the command line. When comparing any tool, ask:.

Recent findings suggest that features such as search by capture time, folder or AI-based tagging depend on metadata surviving the loss, and they narrow results without proving a file is intact. Treat them as convenience, not verification.

In a recent development, recovering a video file does not necessarily mean recovering a playable video. A recording interrupted during writing can lack the structural information a player needs, and other files may be damaged in ways that block playback.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction matters. Recovery retrieves missing or inaccessible data, while repair tries to fix damage that affects a file’s usability. Some cases need one, the other or both. Repair has limits too: if essential video data was overwritten or never recorded, software cannot recreate the original footage in full. After any recovery or repair, play the file all the way through and compare it with what you expect.

For a quick check of a recovered clip, ffprobe can show whether the container is readable:.

An error or a missing duration suggests the file needs repair or is incomplete.

Often yes, if nothing has overwritten them. Stop using the card immediately and scan it or an image of it.

In a recent development, not before recovery. Formatting changes file system structures and may make recovery harder.

It has been revealed that recovery retrieves missing data. Repair fixes a file that exists but will not open or play correctly.

Not always. PhotoRec and TestDisk are free and open source, while paid tools add a graphical interface and extras such as previews, filtering and video repair.

On a different drive from the card. Saving to the same card can overwrite data you still want.

It has been revealed that SD card data loss creates two related challenges: getting files back, and working out which recovered files are useful. Stopping use of the card, working on an image and understanding the difference between file system recovery, carving and repair put you in a better position, whichever tool you choose. Graphical tools aim to make large result sets easier to navigate, and free tools such as PhotoRec and TestDisk remain solid options. Try your chosen tool on a copy first, verify what you recover, and keep a backup so you do not need to do this again.

Tech Report: Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (286 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence.
  • Industry observers note that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths.
  • Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence. In LLM RL, the model serves as the policy, π(action | previous tokens), and true on-policy learning requires every action in an upgrade to be generated and evaluated by that exact same policy. While a synchronous loop ensures each rollout batch is scored using the same weights that generated it, a critical numerical requirement remains: the sampler and trainer must evaluate that policy identically.

Industry observers note that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths. The sampler chooses each action token during incremental decoding and records its behavior logprob. The trainer evaluates the same token in batched forward-backward passes to compute its current logprob and gradients. Under the same weights, these differing execution paths can still assign different logprobs to the same token and context. The training schedule is on-policy, but the numerical execution has introduced a hidden off-policy gap that compounds over multi-turn trajectories.

Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

Industry observers note that A reduction is a tree of floating-point additions. Floating-point addition is not associative, so changing the tree changes where rounding occurs. The effect is easier to expose in bfloat16, which retains less precision than float32.

What an AI Marketing Agent Actually Does, and How to Build a Guarded One
